title: Football Movement Preparation Flow
objective: Develop a progressive football-based warm-up that prepares players to run, change direction, handle the football and communicate before higher-intensity training.
groundSize: A rectangular area approximately 35 metres long and 25 metres wide.
equipment: One football for every two players
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a 35-metre by 25-metre rectangle.
Divide the rectangle into four five-to-eight-metre movement lanes using cones.
Pair players with one football between each pair.
Position pairs evenly around the outside of the area.
Allocate one movement activity to each lane: mobility, running mechanics, ball movement and controlled change of direction.
Leave a central recovery area where players can walk, reset and receive instructions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Pairs begin by moving around the boundary at walking pace while handballing every three to four steps.
On the coach’s signal, players enter the first lane and complete dynamic mobility movements such as walking lunges, hip openings or controlled leg swings while carrying the football.
In the second lane, players perform low-intensity running mechanics including high knees, heel recovery and gradual acceleration.
In the third lane, players move the football by hand and foot while maintaining continuous movement and communication.
In the fourth lane, players complete controlled deceleration, lateral movement and gentle changes of direction.
After completing all four lanes, players walk through the central recovery area for 20–30 seconds.
Repeat the sequence two or three times, increasing movement speed from approximately 40 per cent to 70 per cent.
Finish with two progressive 25-metre run-throughs while carrying or receiving the football.
coachingPoints: Increase intensity gradually rather than beginning with fast running.
Keep players upright, balanced and relaxed through all movements.
Use short steps when preparing to change direction or slow down.
Encourage players to scan before receiving the football.
Maintain accurate handballs and kicks even during simple movement preparation.
Keep communication continuous between partners.
Ensure mobility movements remain controlled and do not become rushed.
Adjust movement ranges for players returning from injury or managing restricted mobility.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players increase speed progressively rather than moving too hard too early.
Whether running posture and foot placement remain controlled.
Whether players complete football skills without stopping their movement.
Whether players communicate before delivering or receiving the football.
Whether older or returning players require modified movement ranges.

commonErrors.error: Players begin at near-maximum pace.
commonErrors.correction: Set clear intensity targets for each round and require the first round to remain controlled.

commonErrors.error: Players rush mobility movements.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce movement speed and prioritise posture and range over distance covered.

commonErrors.error: Football disposal becomes careless.
commonErrors.correction: Require the receiver to call before every handball or kick.

commonErrors.error: Players use long steps when changing direction.
commonErrors.correction: Coach shorter preparation steps and a lower centre of gravity.

commonErrors.error: Players stand still during explanations.
commonErrors.correction: Keep instructions brief and use walking recovery while coaching.

progressions: Add reactive movement calls using coloured cones.
Introduce short kicking exchanges during the final round.
Increase the final run-throughs to 75–80 per cent intensity.
Add a chasing partner during selected acceleration movements.
regressions: Remove kicking and use handball only.
Reduce the movement area and total number of repetitions.
Replace lateral and change-of-direction movements with straight-line walking.
Allow players with mobility restrictions to work through a separate modified lane.
successIndicators: Increase intensity progressively without visible loss of movement quality.
Complete clean football skills while moving.
Maintain balance during acceleration, deceleration and direction changes.
Finish ready for the main session rather than fatigued.
matchApplication: Australian football requires players to accelerate, decelerate, turn, receive and dispose of the football from the opening contest. This drill prepares the body and mind for those actions while keeping the warm-up connected to football skills.

title: Continuous Possession Conditioning Loop
objective: Develop the ability to maintain continuous low-intensity movement while executing clean football skills and rotating through supporting positions.
groundSize: A 40-metre by 30-metre rectangle.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark four possession stations around the perimeter of the rectangle.
Place one or two players at each station.
Position the remaining players evenly between stations as moving support players.
Begin with one football for every four players.
Establish a clockwise movement direction for the first round.
Create a five-metre central zone that players must avoid unless changing sides.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player at the first station kicks 12–18 metres to a moving player leading towards the next station.
The receiver marks, continues forward and handballs to a supporting runner.
The supporting runner carries the football for five to eight metres before kicking to the next station.
Every player follows their disposal and rotates into the next position.
The football continues around the loop without stopping.
Players work at approximately 50–60 per cent running intensity.
After two minutes, reverse the movement direction.
Complete three to five continuous work periods with 30 seconds of walking recovery between periods.
Add footballs only when the group can maintain spacing and accuracy.
coachingPoints: Keep players moving before, during and after possession.
Lead towards the football rather than waiting at a cone.
Deliver kicks to the receiver’s forward side.
Time support runs so the handball option arrives after the mark.
Follow every disposal immediately.
Maintain enough spacing to avoid queues at stations.
Use relaxed running at a sustainable intensity.
Preserve disposal quality rather than rushing to increase speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players remain active after disposing of the football.
Whether station queues develop because rotations are poorly timed.
Whether support runners arrive too early or too late.
Whether kicking accuracy is maintained throughout each work period.
Whether the running intensity remains controlled and sustainable.

commonErrors.error: Players wait flat-footed at stations.
commonErrors.correction: Require each receiver to begin a short lead before the kick is released.

commonErrors.error: Too many players gather at one station.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust starting numbers and require immediate follow-through after disposal.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint early and then walk.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce an even 50–60 per cent running pace.

commonErrors.error: Handball receivers run alongside the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Create depth and arrive from behind or at an angle.

commonErrors.error: Extra footballs create congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Remove one football until spacing and timing improve.

progressions: Add a second disposal option at each station.
Require the receiver to choose between handball and kick.
Increase the work period from two minutes to three minutes.
Add passive defenders inside the rectangle to influence passing lanes.
Finish each possession chain with a 20-metre acceleration before rejoining.
regressions: Use handball only around a smaller area.
successIndicators: Maintain continuous movement throughout each interval.
Complete accurate short kicks and handballs.
Finish each interval able to repeat the same workload.
matchApplication: The drill develops the low-intensity movement that occurs between high-speed involvements in Australian football. Players learn to remain available, support possession and maintain skill quality without unnecessarily sprinting during every phase.

title: Work-to-Rest Football Intervals
objective: Teach players to complete defined football work periods at a controlled intensity and use recovery periods effectively before repeating the effort.
groundSize: Two or more 30-metre by 15-metre lanes.
equipment: One football for every three players
Coloured bibs if multiple groups are used
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark parallel lanes 30 metres long and 15 metres wide.
Place groups of three at one end of each lane.
Each group has one football.
Mark a halfway cone at 15 metres and an end cone at 30 metres.
Establish a work period of 40 seconds and a recovery period of 40 seconds for the first round.
Assign players as ball carrier, receiver and supporting runner.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the whistle, the ball carrier runs towards the halfway cone and handballs to the receiver.
The receiver continues to the end cone and kicks back to the supporting runner.
Players continue moving the football up and down the lane for the full work period.
Players must keep moving but should operate at approximately 65–70 per cent intensity.
At the end of 40 seconds, players walk within their lane, control their breathing and reset their positions.
Repeat four intervals.
Change to 45 seconds work and 30 seconds recovery for the second set.
Rotate the starting roles after every interval.
End the drill if skill quality falls below the standard set by the coach.
coachingPoints: Explain the required work and recovery times before starting.
Encourage an even pace rather than an unsustainable first effort.
Keep disposal distances appropriate to the lane.
Use the recovery period actively by walking and controlling breathing.
Reset the football and player positions before the next whistle.
Maintain communication despite increasing breathing rate.
Monitor players individually rather than expecting identical running output.
Stop or modify the drill if movement mechanics deteriorate.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players understand when to work and when to recover.
Whether the first interval is completed too hard.
Whether skill quality remains stable across repeated intervals.
Whether players use recovery actively rather than standing still.
Whether players are ready in position before the next work period.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint the first 15 seconds and fade.
commonErrors.correction: Set a controlled pace target and require the final 10 seconds to match the first 10 seconds.

commonErrors.error: Players stand still during recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Require continuous walking and controlled breathing.

commonErrors.error: Players are not ready when work restarts.
commonErrors.correction: Use the final 10 seconds of recovery to reset positions.

commonErrors.error: Kicks become too long under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce short, achievable disposals within the lane.

commonErrors.error: All groups are forced to use the same intensity.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust distances or tempo for age, fitness and return-to-play status.

progressions: Reduce recovery to 25 seconds.
Increase work periods to 50–60 seconds.
Add a decision at the halfway cone.
Require a five-metre acceleration after each disposal.
Use different interval formats for separate positional groups.
regressions: Use 30 seconds work and 45 seconds recovery.
Allow walking during the second half of each work period.
Reduce the number of total intervals.
successIndicators: Maintain an even work rate throughout each interval.
Begin the next repetition in the correct position.
Preserve disposal accuracy across the set.
Demonstrate an understanding of pacing rather than treating every effort as a sprint.
matchApplication: Australian football is intermittent. Players repeatedly work, recover and re-enter play rather than running at one constant speed. This drill introduces the discipline required to manage effort and recover between involvements.

title: Four-Station Aerobic Football Circuit
objective: Develop general aerobic football capacity by rotating players through continuous skill stations that require different movement and disposal patterns.
groundSize: Approximately one-third of an oval or a 60-metre by 50-metre area.
equipment: Four portable targets or marker gates
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Create four stations around the area:
Station 1: Short kick, follow and receive.
Station 2: Ground-ball collection, handball and support run.
Station 3: Lead, mark and return kick.
Station 4: Carry, bounce and kick through a target gate.
Place three to six players at each station. Allocate two minutes of work at each station followed by 30 seconds to rotate.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their allocated station on the whistle.
At Station 1, players kick 15 metres, follow the kick and receive a return handball.
At Station 2, players collect a rolling football, handball to a partner and run past to receive again.
At Station 3, players make a 10–15-metre lead, mark and kick back to the feeder.
At Station 4, players carry the football for 20 metres, take one bounce and kick through a target gate.
Players continue their station activity for two minutes.
On the coach’s signal, players walk or jog to the next station within 30 seconds.
Complete all four stations.
Rest for two minutes, then repeat the circuit in the opposite direction or with revised skill demands.
Record group accuracy or completion targets where appropriate.
coachingPoints: Keep players moving continuously without turning the circuit into maximal running.
Organise enough footballs to prevent waiting.
Use clean, realistic skill execution at every station.
Encourage players to follow their disposal.
Maintain safe spacing between separate stations.
Use transition time to move and recover rather than stand.
Adjust station distances for different age or conditioning groups.
Prioritise consistent work across the full circuit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players are active for most of each station period.
Whether queues form because station design is inefficient.
Whether skill quality changes between the first and fourth station.
Whether players transition promptly when the whistle sounds.
Whether each station creates a distinct football movement demand.

commonErrors.error: Players wait too long between repetitions.
commonErrors.correction: Add footballs, split lines or create a second working lane.

commonErrors.error: Players treat one station as a sprint.
commonErrors.correction: Set a consistent aerobic pace for all four stations.

commonErrors.error: Station transitions become disorganised.
commonErrors.correction: Use colour-coded stations and a fixed rotation direction.

commonErrors.error: Players complete skills without following the disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Make follow-through movement part of every station rule.

commonErrors.error: Technique deteriorates late in the circuit.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce station duration or simplify the skill demand.

progressions: Increase station duration to two and a half or three minutes.
Add a passive defender at one or two stations.
Introduce scoring targets for accuracy.
Reduce transition recovery to 20 seconds.
Add a fifth station involving change of direction.
regressions: Reduce the circuit to three stations.
Run separate modified stations for younger or returning players.
successIndicators: Maintain accurate disposal and clean ball handling.
Work at a sustainable intensity across the circuit.
Demonstrate similar movement quality in the final station as the first.
matchApplication: The circuit reflects the varied low-to-moderate intensity tasks players complete across a match, including leading, supporting, collecting, carrying and disposing. It develops the capacity to move continuously while repeatedly performing football skills.
relatedDrills: CF-008 – Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue

title: First-Five Acceleration with Football
objective: Develop efficient acceleration over the first five to ten metres while integrating realistic football starts, pickups and disposals.
groundSize: Three to six acceleration lanes, each 15 metres long and five metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark parallel 15-metre lanes.
Place a starting cone, a five-metre cone and a ten-metre cone in each lane.
Position one feeder five metres to the side of each lane.
Place a football on the ground or in the feeder’s hands depending on the repetition.
Organise players in groups of three or four.
Allow players to walk back after each effort.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player begins in an athletic stance at the starting cone.
On the coach’s visual or verbal cue, the player accelerates through the first five metres.
The player completes one of four actions:
Collect a stationary football.
Receive a handball.
Chase a rolling football.
Accelerate after making a short handball.
The player continues through the ten-metre cone before controlling their speed.
The player completes a short kick or handball to the feeder.
Players walk back outside the lane.
Complete two repetitions of each starting action.
Allow at least 30–40 seconds between high-quality efforts.
Finish with two reactive races in which the coach selects the football action late.
coachingPoints: Begin with the body leaning slightly forward from the ankles.
Drive strongly through the first three steps.
Use powerful arm action without crossing the body.
Keep the first steps short and forceful.
Accelerate through the football rather than reaching from a stationary position.
Lower the hips before collecting a ground ball.
Keep the head and chest stable when receiving.
Provide enough recovery to preserve acceleration quality.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players generate forward movement immediately.
Whether the first step is too long.
Whether players slow down before collecting or receiving.
Whether posture remains stable through the acceleration.
Whether recovery time is sufficient for repeated quality efforts.

commonErrors.error: First step is too long and causes braking.
commonErrors.correction: Coach shorter, more powerful opening steps.

commonErrors.error: Players rise upright immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a gradual rise through the first five metres.

commonErrors.error: Players reach down for the football and stop their feet.
commonErrors.correction: Run through the pickup with the body moving forward.

commonErrors.error: Too many repetitions are completed without recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Increase walk-back distance or reduce players per lane.

commonErrors.error: Players race beyond technical control.
commonErrors.correction: Remove competition until movement quality improves.

progressions: Use random visual cues to select the lane or football action.
Add a trailing shadow defender.
Increase the acceleration distance to 15 metres.
Begin from prone, kneeling or lateral positions.
Require a kick immediately after the acceleration.
regressions: Begin from a standing staggered stance.
Reduce the number of repetitions for Over 35 or returning players.
successIndicators: Maintain control when collecting or receiving.
Execute a clean disposal after accelerating.
Repeat high-quality efforts without visible technical decline.
matchApplication: The first five metres often determine whether a player reaches a loose football, creates separation, applies pressure or receives in space. This drill connects acceleration technique with common Australian football possession actions.

title: Brake, Balance and Re-Accelerate
objective: Develop the ability to slow down under control, maintain balance and accelerate into a new direction while retaining possession of the football.
groundSize: Four to six channels measuring 20 metres by eight metres.
equipment: One football for every two players
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a starting cone at one end of each channel.
Place a deceleration zone between the eight-metre and twelve-metre marks.
Position red, blue and yellow exit gates five metres beyond the deceleration zone.
Place a receiver outside each exit gate.
Players begin with a football at the starting cone.
Keep lanes separated to prevent collisions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier accelerates from the starting cone at approximately 70 per cent.
On entering the deceleration zone, the player reduces speed using several short steps.
The coach calls or displays an exit-gate colour.
The player plants outside the deceleration zone and re-accelerates towards the nominated gate.
After passing through the gate, the player handballs or kicks to the receiver.
The receiver returns the football and joins the starting line.
The original ball carrier rotates to the receiver position.
Complete three repetitions in each direction.
Increase speed only when players demonstrate control.
Finish with two reactive repetitions in which the gate is called later.
coachingPoints: Begin slowing before the final plant step.
Use several short braking steps rather than one heavy step.
Lower the hips while keeping the chest stable.
Keep the knees aligned over the feet.
Carry the football securely during the change of direction.
Scan for the exit cue while decelerating.
Push forcefully away from the outside foot.
Rebuild speed after balance has been established.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players begin decelerating early enough.
Whether knees collapse inward during braking or planting.
Whether players remain balanced while carrying the football.
Whether players can scan without losing movement control.
Whether the re-acceleration is decisive after the direction change.

commonErrors.error: Player attempts to stop on one step.
commonErrors.correction: Mark a wider braking zone and require three or more short steps.

commonErrors.error: Player remains too upright.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips before the direction change.

commonErrors.error: Player plants with the foot too far outside the body.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the foot closer to the centre of mass.

commonErrors.error: Player looks down throughout the movement.
commonErrors.correction: Display the exit cue at chest height.

commonErrors.error: Disposal is rushed immediately after turning.
commonErrors.correction: Require two balanced acceleration steps before disposing.

progressions: Increase approach speed.
Add a passive defender closing from behind.
Allow the player to choose the best exit gate.
Add a bounce before the braking zone.
Require a kick to a moving target after re-acceleration.
regressions: Complete the drill without a football.
successIndicators: Maintain knee, hip and trunk alignment.
Re-accelerate without slipping or extra adjustment steps.
Complete an accurate disposal after changing direction.
matchApplication: Players must repeatedly brake, evade, change direction and accelerate again when avoiding pressure, adjusting to a loose football or creating a new disposal lane. Efficient deceleration also reduces unnecessary physical stress and improves movement safety.

title: Introductory Repeat-Effort Football Runs
objective: Introduce repeated football efforts with enough recovery to maintain running mechanics, decision quality and clean skill execution.
groundSize: Four to seven lanes measuring 25 metres by eight metres.
equipment: Bibs if groups are divided by capacity
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a starting line, a 10-metre football station and a 25-metre end line.
Place one feeder at the football station.
Organise three or four players in each lane.
Divide players into appropriate conditioning groups where necessary.
Set the introductory format at four efforts with 25–35 seconds between efforts and two minutes between sets.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player begins at the starting line.
On the whistle, the player accelerates to the 10-metre station.
The feeder rolls or handballs the football into the player’s path.
The player collects or receives, disposes back to the feeder and continues to the 25-metre line.
The player turns under control and jogs back to the start.
The next effort begins after 25–35 seconds.
Complete four efforts in the first set.
Rest for two minutes while walking and controlling breathing.
Complete a second set using the opposite disposal side or a different football action.
Record whether running time and skill quality remain consistent across the set.
coachingPoints: Treat the drill as repeated quality efforts, not one maximal effort followed by poor repetitions.
Accelerate strongly through the first ten metres.
Execute the football skill without stopping.
Turn under control at the end line.
Use the return jog as the beginning of recovery.
Keep effort times within a narrow range.
Maintain posture and foot placement late in the set.
Modify distances or repetition numbers for younger, older or returning players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether effort speed changes significantly across the set.
Whether the player slows before receiving or collecting.
Whether the turn at the end line remains controlled.
Whether football skill deteriorates before running speed.
Whether the prescribed recovery is appropriate for each group.

commonErrors.error: First effort is excessively fast.
commonErrors.correction: Set the target as repeatable high-quality speed rather than a maximal sprint.

commonErrors.error: Player stops to receive the football.
commonErrors.correction: Deliver the football into the player’s running path.

commonErrors.error: Player turns sharply on one leg at the end line.
commonErrors.correction: Use a wider turning zone and several control steps.

commonErrors.error: Recovery becomes standing and bending over.
commonErrors.correction: Require walking and controlled breathing.

commonErrors.error: Later repetitions become technically unsafe.
commonErrors.correction: End the set or increase recovery before quality falls further.

progressions: Add a fifth or sixth effort.
Reduce recovery between repetitions by five seconds.
Add a second football action on the return movement.
Introduce a passive chasing opponent.
Use positional distances appropriate to midfielders, key-position players and small forwards.
regressions: Replace the return jog with a walk.
successIndicators: Complete all efforts within the coach’s consistency target.
Execute the football skill without stopping.
Maintain safe acceleration and turning mechanics.
Finish the final repetition with similar intent to the first.
matchApplication: Australian football frequently demands two, three or four efforts in one passage, including chasing, supporting, pressuring and rejoining play. This drill introduces repeat-effort conditioning without allowing fatigue to override safe movement or clean football skills.

title: Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue
objective: Develop the ability to regain composure and execute clean football skills immediately after a controlled conditioning effort.
groundSize: A 35-metre by 30-metre area.
equipment: One football for every three players
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a 15-metre running loop on one side of the area.
Mark a 20-metre skill channel beside the loop.
Place one feeder and one target player in each skill channel.
Organise groups of three.
Position two coloured target gates at the end of each channel.
Set each repetition to include 15–20 seconds of controlled running followed immediately by a football skill sequence.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player completes one controlled lap of the running loop at approximately 70 per cent intensity.
The player enters the skill channel and receives a handball from the feeder.
The feeder calls one of the two coloured target gates.
The player takes two or three control steps and kicks through the nominated gate to the target player.
The player follows the kick and becomes the target.
The target retrieves the football and becomes the feeder.
The feeder moves to the running start.
Complete four repetitions per player.
In the second round, replace the handball receive with a rolling ground ball.
Allow 45–60 seconds between each player’s working repetitions.
coachingPoints: Use fatigue that is noticeable but does not destroy technique.
Regain balance before disposing of the football.
Control breathing without delaying the decision.
Scan and identify the correct target quickly.
Take the football cleanly with the hands in front.
Use a compact kicking action over short distance.
Follow the disposal to maintain movement.
Adjust the running dose if accuracy drops sharply.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players rush their disposal after the running effort.
Whether the first touch is clean.
Whether players can identify the correct target while breathing heavily.
Whether kicking mechanics change under light fatigue.
Whether the conditioning dose remains appropriate.

commonErrors.error: Player kicks immediately without regaining balance.
commonErrors.correction: Require two controlled steps before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Player looks only at the football.
commonErrors.correction: Call the target colour before the receive so the player must scan.

commonErrors.error: Running effort is too hard for the skill objective.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce loop distance or running speed.

commonErrors.error: Player slows excessively before entering the skill channel.
commonErrors.correction: Run through the transition cone and settle during the first two possession steps.

commonErrors.error: Accuracy collapses across the group.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery or shorten the conditioning effort.

progressions: Add a passive defender to pressure the disposal.
Increase the number of target options to three.
Require a handball receive, ground-ball collection and kick in the same repetition.
Reduce recovery between repetitions.
Add a second disposal after the first target receives.
regressions: Remove the running loop and use a short acceleration only.
Use handball through the target instead of kicking.
Increase disposal distance only after accuracy improves.
Allow additional recovery for Over 35 or returning players.
successIndicators: Regain balance quickly after the running effort.
Maintain acceptable kicking or handball accuracy.
Show only minimal technical decline across repetitions.
matchApplication: Players regularly dispose of the football after chasing, leading, pressing or supporting. The ability to settle, scan and execute under manageable fatigue is essential to retaining possession and making effective decisions.

title: Recover, Reset and Re-enter
primarySkill: Recovery and reset habits between football efforts
objective: Teach players to use short recovery periods effectively, regain positional awareness and re-enter the next football effort with purpose.
groundSize: A 45-metre by 35-metre area divided into three zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Divide the area into a work zone, recovery zone and re-entry zone.
Organise groups of three.
In each group, assign one ball carrier, one support player and one target.
Place a reset cone in the recovery zone.
Position two re-entry gates at different angles.
The coach controls work and recovery periods.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier and support player complete a 20-second possession movement through the work zone.
The passage ends with a kick to the target.
All three players immediately enter the recovery zone.
Players walk, control breathing and communicate their next roles.
During the final five seconds of recovery, the coach calls a re-entry gate.
Players move into the re-entry zone and begin the next possession through that gate.
Roles rotate after every effort.
Use 20 seconds work and 25 seconds recovery for six repetitions.
In later rounds, reduce recovery to 20 seconds.
Award one point when the group is organised and moving through the correct gate before the next work whistle.
coachingPoints: Begin recovery immediately after the football action.
Keep moving at walking pace rather than stopping.
Use slow, controlled breathing.
Communicate the next roles early.
Scan the coach, football and re-entry gates during recovery.
Use the final seconds of recovery to prepare movement.
Re-enter with intent rather than drifting into position.
Recognise that recovery includes physical, mental and positional reset.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players stop completely after the work effort.
Whether communication occurs during recovery.
Whether players identify their next role.
Whether re-entry begins before or after the whistle.
Whether recovery habits improve across the drill.

commonErrors.error: Players bend over or sit during short recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Require walking recovery with upright posture.

commonErrors.error: Players remain silent between repetitions.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate one player to call the next roles.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for the whistle before organising.
commonErrors.correction: Use the final five seconds as a compulsory setup period.

commonErrors.error: Players re-enter through the wrong gate.
commonErrors.correction: Require all players to point or call the gate before moving.

commonErrors.error: Recovery pace becomes another hard effort.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that the recovery zone is controlled walking only.

progressions: Shorten the recovery period.
Add a second football to increase scanning demand.
Allow the coach to change the gate during the final three seconds.
Introduce a passive opponent during re-entry.
Add positional roles such as inside midfielder, winger and forward.
regressions: Reduce each work period to 15 seconds.
successIndicators: Restart the next effort organised and ready.
matchApplication: Players must recover while the match continues around them. Effective players use low-intensity moments to breathe, scan, communicate, regain structure and prepare for the next contest rather than becoming disconnected from play.
relatedDrills: CF-008 – Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue

title: Conditioning Fundamentals Assessment
objective: Assess whether players can apply the fundamental physical, technical and recovery behaviours introduced in CF-001 to CF-009 within one integrated football-conditioning activity.
groundSize: Approximately one-third to one-half of an oval.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create five connected assessment zones:
Preparation Zone: Dynamic movement with football.
Continuous Movement Zone: Low-intensity possession loop.
Acceleration and Braking Zone: Five-metre acceleration, controlled deceleration and directional exit.
Repeat-Effort Zone: Three repeated 20-metre football efforts.
Fatigue Skill and Recovery Zone: Target disposal followed by active recovery and organised re-entry.
Divide players into groups of four to six.
Start each group at a different zone.
Allocate three minutes at each zone with 45 seconds to rotate.
Prepare a simple assessment sheet covering movement quality, effort control, football skill, recovery behaviour and communication.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete the Preparation Zone at a progressively increasing intensity.
In the Continuous Movement Zone, players maintain possession while moving at a sustainable aerobic pace.
In the Acceleration and Braking Zone, each player accelerates, controls their speed, changes direction and disposes to a target.
In the Repeat-Effort Zone, players complete three short football efforts with prescribed recovery.
In the Fatigue Skill and Recovery Zone, players complete a running effort, execute a target disposal, walk through recovery and organise for re-entry.
Coaches assess players against the same behaviours taught in CF-001 to CF-009.
After three minutes, groups rotate clockwise.
Complete all five zones.
Allow three minutes of recovery.
Repeat selected zones where the coach requires further observation.
Finish with a short group review identifying one conditioning strength and one improvement priority.
coachingPoints: Assess football-conditioning behaviour rather than running speed alone.
Observe whether players prepare progressively before harder efforts.
Reward repeatable effort rather than one exceptional repetition.
Monitor acceleration and deceleration mechanics.
Record skill quality before and after fatigue.
Assess whether players recover actively and prepare for the next effort.
Note communication and positional awareness during low-intensity periods.
Apply appropriate standards for age, position, training history and injury status.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players move progressively through preparation.
Whether players can sustain continuous football movement.
Whether acceleration and deceleration remain balanced.
Whether repeated efforts remain consistent.
Whether football skill deteriorates under light fatigue.
Whether players use recovery periods effectively.
Whether players communicate and reset before the next task.
Whether individual modifications are required.

commonErrors.error: Assessment focuses only on running time.
commonErrors.correction: Score physical, technical, decision and recovery behaviours separately.

commonErrors.error: Players treat every zone as maximal.
commonErrors.correction: Explain the required intensity and purpose of each zone.

commonErrors.error: Coaches attempt to observe too many details at once.
commonErrors.correction: Assign one or two assessment categories to each coach.

commonErrors.error: Players compare raw results across different age or positional groups.
commonErrors.correction: Use individual standards and appropriate group benchmarks.

commonErrors.error: Skill errors are ignored because the running effort is strong.
commonErrors.correction: Make skill quality a required component of the assessment.

commonErrors.error: Players stop completely during rotation periods.
commonErrors.correction: Require walking recovery and immediate organisation for the next zone.

progressions: Add controlled defensive pressure in selected zones.
Reduce transition time between zones.
Add position-specific running and disposal requirements.
Record times, accuracy and repeat-effort variation.
Repeat the assessment after a four-to-six-week conditioning block.
regressions: Reduce the assessment to three zones.
Remove the repeat-effort zone for younger players.
Use handball instead of kicking in the fatigue skill zone.
Conduct separate assessments for modified and return-to-play groups.
successIndicators: Maintain sustainable movement through continuous football activity.
Accelerate, decelerate and change direction safely.
Repeat efforts without major loss of running quality.
Execute football skills under light fatigue.
Recover actively and organise for the next effort.
Demonstrate a clear individual conditioning baseline.
matchApplication: The assessment combines the fundamental conditioning demands of Australian football: movement preparation, continuous positioning, short acceleration, controlled braking, repeated efforts, skill execution under fatigue and rapid recovery between involvements. It provides coaches with a football-relevant baseline for planning future conditioning work.

title: Tempo Lane Ball Movement
objective: Develop the ability to maintain a prescribed running tempo while completing continuous football skills and supporting movement.
groundSize: Four to six lanes measuring 40 metres by eight metres.
equipment: One football for every four players
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark parallel 40-metre lanes.
Place tempo markers at 10-metre intervals.
Organise groups of four in each lane.
Position two players at each end of the lane.
Allocate one football to each group.
Establish three movement tempos: controlled jog, steady run and strong run.
Explain that players must match the required tempo rather than race.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player runs from one end of the lane while carrying the football.
At the first marker, the player handballs to a teammate moving from the opposite end.
Both players continue through the lane and exchange another handball at the halfway point.
The receiving player finishes with a short kick to the next player waiting at the end.
Players rotate immediately and continue the pattern.
Complete two minutes at a controlled jog.
Rest for 30 seconds while walking.
Complete two minutes at a steady running tempo.
Rest for 30 seconds.
Complete one minute at a strong but repeatable tempo.
Reverse the handballing and kicking sides for the final set.
coachingPoints: Match the nominated tempo rather than running faster than required.
Keep stride length relaxed and efficient.
Maintain clean handballs in front of the moving receiver.
Deliver kicks before reaching the end cone.
Continue moving after every disposal.
Use the recovery period to walk and reset.
Keep group spacing even throughout the lane.
Maintain similar movement quality at all three tempos.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players understand and maintain different running tempos.
Whether faster players disrupt the spacing of the group.
Whether disposal quality changes as tempo increases.
Whether players continue moving after disposing.
Whether the strong tempo remains repeatable rather than maximal.

commonErrors.error: Players race during the controlled phase.
commonErrors.correction: Set a target arrival time for each 10-metre section.

commonErrors.error: Handballs are delivered behind the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Release the football earlier and aim to the receiver’s forward side.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after disposing.
commonErrors.correction: Require every player to continue through the next marker.

commonErrors.error: Groups bunch near the halfway point.
commonErrors.correction: Stagger starting times and reinforce lane spacing.

commonErrors.error: Strong tempo becomes a maximal sprint.
commonErrors.correction: Define the final pace as controlled high-speed running rather than all-out speed.

progressions: Use different tempos within the same repetition.
Add a bounce before the final kick.
Introduce a late handball or kick decision.
Reduce recovery between work periods.
Add a passive trailing defender.
regressions: Complete one tempo level at a time.
Allow younger players to walk the recovery section.
successIndicators: Maintain accurate disposal at each speed.
Complete each set without a major decline in movement quality.
matchApplication: Players must vary their running speed throughout a match. This drill develops the ability to move efficiently at different tempos while remaining involved in possession and support play.
relatedDrills: CF-008 – Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue

title: Aerobic Kick-Mark-Run Waves
primarySkill: Aerobic running through repeated kick-mark involvement
objective: Develop continuous aerobic movement through repeated leading, marking, kicking and follow-up running patterns.
groundSize: Three to five channels measuring 60 metres by 12 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark three stations along each 60-metre channel.
Position players evenly at the start, middle and end stations.
Use one football per channel.
Set lead distances between 12 and 18 metres.
Establish a continuous rotation in which players follow their kick.
Ensure adjacent channels are far enough apart to prevent footballs crossing.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player at the start station leads forward and receives a kick from the middle station.
After marking, the player turns and kicks to a player leading from the end station.
The original kicker follows the disposal to the next station.
The receiver at the end station marks, turns and begins the return wave in the opposite direction.
Players continue rotating through all three stations.
Complete three minutes of continuous work.
Walk for 45 seconds.
Repeat for three or four sets.
Change the required kicking foot or lead angle between sets.
Coaches may count completed uncontested marks as a group accuracy measure.
coachingPoints: Begin the lead before the kicker is ready to dispose.
Accelerate into the lead and control speed before marking.
Kick to the receiver’s advantage.
Follow every kick immediately.
Maintain an even running effort throughout the set.
Keep the channel wide enough for safe turning.
Use clear verbal and visual communication.
Prioritise rhythm and continuity over maximum speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether receivers time their leads effectively.
Whether players follow their kick without delay.
Whether marks are taken at running speed.
Whether kicking accuracy remains stable late in each set.
Whether players maintain a sustainable aerobic pace.

commonErrors.error: Receivers begin their lead too late.
commonErrors.correction: Start moving as the previous mark is completed.

commonErrors.error: Kickers wait after disposing.
commonErrors.correction: Make following the kick compulsory.

commonErrors.error: Players drift across neighbouring channels.
commonErrors.correction: Use clear side boundaries and directional cones.

commonErrors.error: Marks are taken flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Require the receiver to move through the marking point.

commonErrors.error: Early running pace cannot be sustained.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce first-minute intensity and target an even effort.

progressions: Add angled leads rather than straight-line leads.
Require the receiver to play on immediately.
Introduce one passive defender in each channel.
Increase set duration to four minutes.
Add a handball receive before the kick.
successIndicators: Maintain continuous running for the full set.
matchApplication: Players repeatedly lead, mark, dispose and continue running to support the next phase. This drill develops the aerobic capacity and work habits required to remain connected across multiple possessions.

title: Handball Support Shuttle
objective: Develop the ability to repeatedly handball, accelerate past possession and provide the next support option.
groundSize: Three to six lanes measuring 25 metres by eight metres.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a starting cone, halfway cone and end cone in each lane.
Organise three players in each lane.
Position two players at the start and one at the end.
Give the first player at the start a football.
Establish a work period of 30 seconds and recovery period of 45 seconds.
Ensure players have sufficient space beyond each end cone to slow down.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A handballs to Player B and accelerates forward.
Player B runs three to five metres and handballs back to Player A.
Player A continues forward and handballs to Player C at the far end.
Player B continues running to support Player C.
The pattern immediately returns in the opposite direction.
Players rotate naturally through the three positions.
Continue for 30 seconds.
Walk for 45 seconds.
Complete four to six repetitions.
Change the initiating hand between repetitions.
coachingPoints: Accelerate immediately after handballing.
Run past the receiver rather than stopping beside them.
Deliver the football in front of the support runner.
Keep hands ready while moving.
Use direct running lines.
Communicate before every receive.
Maintain control near the end cones.
Use recovery to prepare for the next repetition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players accelerate after disposing.
Whether the return handball is delivered to space.
Whether players stop after receiving.
Whether running lines are direct.
Whether skill quality remains consistent across repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Player handballs and watches.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate acceleration after release.

commonErrors.error: Support runner passes too close to the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Create one to two metres of lateral separation.

commonErrors.error: Handball is delivered behind the runner.
commonErrors.correction: Release earlier and target the runner’s forward hand.

commonErrors.error: Players turn sharply at full speed.
commonErrors.correction: Add a larger turning zone beyond the end cone.

commonErrors.error: Groups lose structure late in the repetition.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten work time or increase recovery.

progressions: Increase work time to 40 seconds.
Reduce recovery to 30 seconds.
Add a passive defender in the middle section.
Require a change of direction before the return movement.
Add a fourth player and a second support option.
regressions: Walk or jog the return movement.
successIndicators: Deliver handballs to the receiver’s advantage.
Repeat the movement without significant skill decline.
matchApplication: Give-and-go handball chains are used to escape congestion, create overlap and break defensive lines. This drill develops the repeated support running required to remain involved after the first disposal.
relatedDrills: CF-008 – Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue

title: Ground-Ball Conditioning Grid
primarySkill: Repeated ground-ball collection under controlled fatigue
objective: Develop repeated movement to ground balls while maintaining safe body position, clean collection and accurate release.
groundSize: A 30-metre by 30-metre grid divided into four quarters.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Divide the grid into four equal quarters.
Place a feeder on the outside of each quarter.
Position two to four working players in each quarter.
Place a target cone on the opposite side of each feeder.
Give each feeder two footballs.
Establish a 25-second work period and 40-second recovery period.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder rolls a football into the quarter.
The working player accelerates, decelerates and collects the football cleanly.
The player handballs back to the feeder.
The player then runs around the target cone before returning for another ground ball.
The feeder varies the direction and speed of each roll.
Continue for 25 seconds.
Players walk and recover for 40 seconds.
Rotate feeders after every repetition.
Complete four to six repetitions.
Change the required release hand during the second half of the drill.
coachingPoints: Approach the football with controlled speed.
Lower the hips rather than bending only at the waist.
Keep the body behind the football.
Use two hands whenever possible.
Collect through the line of the football.
Stabilise before handballing.
Accelerate away after release.
Preserve collection quality as fatigue increases.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players arrive too fast to collect cleanly.
Whether the head remains over the football.
Whether players use two hands.
Whether handball accuracy changes under fatigue.
Whether players accelerate after releasing the football.

commonErrors.error: Player overruns the football.
commonErrors.correction: Begin decelerating two to three steps earlier.

commonErrors.error: Player bends from the waist.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips and knees while keeping the chest strong.

commonErrors.error: Collection is attempted with one hand.
commonErrors.correction: Use two hands unless the football’s path prevents it.

commonErrors.error: Player remains stationary after handballing.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate movement around the target cone.

commonErrors.error: Feeder rolls become unrealistic.
commonErrors.correction: Keep rolls challenging but collectable within the quarter.

progressions: Add a passive opponent applying shadow pressure.
Require a left or right exit after collection.
Increase work time to 30–35 seconds.
Add a short kick after the handball.
Allow two players to compete for alternate ground balls.
regressions: Remove the run around the target cone.
successIndicators: Collect cleanly with appropriate body position.
Maintain technique throughout each work period.
matchApplication: Ground balls often occur after players have already accelerated, chased or changed direction. This drill develops the ability to control the approach and execute cleanly despite repeated movement demands.
relatedDrills: CF-008 – Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue

title: Controlled Shuttle Disposal
objective: Develop the ability to execute accurate disposals during repeated shuttle movements without allowing running fatigue to overwhelm technique.
groundSize: Four to six lanes measuring 30 metres by eight metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark five-metre, ten-metre and fifteen-metre shuttle lines.
Position a feeder at the starting line.
Place a target gate 15–20 metres beyond the starting line.
Organise three or four players in each lane.
Set work periods of 30 seconds with 50 seconds recovery.
Predetermine whether the final disposal is a kick or handball.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player runs to the five-metre line and returns.
The player runs to the ten-metre line and returns.
The player runs to the fifteen-metre line and returns.
On reaching the starting line, the player receives a football from the feeder.
The player takes two control steps and disposes through the target gate.
The player retrieves the football at walking pace.
The next player begins.
Complete three or four repetitions each.
Alternate kicking and handballing rounds.
Record both shuttle completion and disposal accuracy.
coachingPoints: Run at a repeatable high intensity.
Control each turn with short steps.
Avoid crossing the feet when changing direction.
Regain posture before receiving the football.
Keep the disposal routine simple.
Do not rush the final skill.
Use recovery to walk and control breathing.
Stop the repetition if turning mechanics deteriorate.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players maintain safe turning mechanics.
Whether running pace is consistent.
Whether players receive cleanly after the shuttle.
Whether final disposal accuracy declines.
Whether players recover actively between repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Player turns on one extended leg.
commonErrors.correction: Use several short steps and lower the hips before the line.

commonErrors.error: Player receives while off balance.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the turn and establish posture before receiving.

commonErrors.error: Disposal is rushed because the player is fatigued.
commonErrors.correction: Require two control steps before release.

commonErrors.error: First repetition is much faster than later repetitions.
commonErrors.correction: Set a repeatable target time.

commonErrors.error: Players stand still after finishing.
commonErrors.correction: Use football retrieval as active recovery.

progressions: Reduce recovery between repetitions.
Add a target choice after the shuttle.
Require disposal on the non-preferred side.
Add a passive defender approaching the disposal.
Extend the final shuttle to 20 metres.
regressions: Use five-metre and ten-metre shuttles only.
matchApplication: Players often need to execute after repeated defensive or attacking movements. This drill teaches them to regain balance and complete a purposeful disposal rather than allowing fatigue to dictate poor technique.
relatedDrills: CF-008 – Clean Skills Under Light Fatigue

title: Possession Endurance Squares
objective: Develop sustained football movement by requiring players to continually create, use and replace possession options within a defined square.
groundSize: Two or more squares measuring 25 metres by 25 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Organise four to six players in each square.
Begin without defenders.
Nominate one player as the central support option.
Place the other players around the outside.
Use one football in each square.
Establish two-minute possession periods.
Require players to replace the position they have just passed to.
howTheDrillWorks:
An outside player passes to another player within the square.
After disposing, the player moves to replace the receiver’s previous position.
The central player continually leads to provide a short support option.
Players may kick or handball depending on distance.
No player may remain stationary for more than three seconds.
Continue for two minutes.
Walk for 40 seconds.
Rotate the central player.
Complete four possession periods.
Add one passive defender during the final round if the group maintains structure.
coachingPoints: Move immediately after disposal.
Replace space rather than following the football blindly.
Scan before receiving.
Keep passing distances achievable.
Maintain width within the square.
Use the central support option to change angles.
Communicate early.
Work continuously without unnecessary sprinting.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players remain active after disposing.
Whether space is replaced effectively.
Whether the central player provides useful angles.
Whether possession speed remains controlled.
Whether movement becomes crowded late in the interval.

commonErrors.error: Players follow their own pass directly.
commonErrors.correction: Move to the receiver’s previous space or another vacant position.

commonErrors.error: The square collapses around the football.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce width and minimum spacing.

commonErrors.error: The central player stands behind defenders or teammates.
commonErrors.correction: Lead to visible angles on either side of possession.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint constantly and fatigue quickly.
commonErrors.correction: Use controlled movement and accelerate only to create separation.

commonErrors.error: Players hold the football too long.
commonErrors.correction: Introduce a three-second disposal limit.

progressions: Add one active defender.
Add a second football.
Reduce the square size.
Limit players to one type of disposal for a short period.
Award points for completing a set number of passes without losing shape.
successIndicators: Complete clean skills throughout the interval.
matchApplication: Teams retain possession through continuous movement, spacing and replacement of positions. This drill develops the endurance and awareness required to stay available across extended possession chains.

title: Lead, Recover and Repeat
objective: Develop repeated leading efforts followed by disciplined recovery movement and preparation for the next involvement.
groundSize: Four to six channels measuring 35 metres by ten metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place a feeder at one end of each channel.
Mark three lead cones at different angles and distances.
Position a target player 15 metres beyond the lead area.
Organise three or four working players per channel.
Set a work sequence of three leads before rotation.
Allow 40–50 seconds recovery between sequences.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player begins beside the feeder.
On the feeder’s cue, the player leads to the first cone and receives a kick.
The player marks and kicks to the target.
The player recovers at a controlled jog back towards the feeder.
The feeder immediately directs the player to a second lead cone.
The player completes three different leads in the sequence.
After the third disposal, the player walks to recovery.
The target rotates to feeder, the feeder becomes the worker and the worker becomes the target.
Complete three or four sequences each.
Change lead patterns between rounds.
coachingPoints: Accelerate hard into each lead.
Change lead angle rather than repeating one straight line.
Present hands early.
Control speed before marking.
Kick accurately after the mark.
Recover at an appropriate tempo.
Scan the feeder during the recovery movement.
Prepare mentally for the next lead before reaching the start point.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first and third leads have similar intent.
Whether lead angles create separation.
Whether marking remains clean.
Whether recovery movement is controlled.
Whether players are ready for the next cue.

commonErrors.error: Later leads become slower and less decisive.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery or reduce the sequence to two leads.

commonErrors.error: Player runs directly at the feeder.
commonErrors.correction: Use angled lead cones and require separation from the starting line.

commonErrors.error: Player stops completely after kicking.
commonErrors.correction: Begin recovery immediately after disposal.

commonErrors.error: Player watches the target instead of the feeder.
commonErrors.correction: Reconnect vision with the feeder during recovery.

commonErrors.error: Kick quality declines after the second lead.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce running distance or provide longer recovery.

progressions: Add a passive defender.
Allow the feeder to select lead cones randomly.
Extend the sequence to four leads.
Require a ground-ball pickup on one effort.
Reduce recovery between sequences.
successIndicators: Repeat the sequence with consistent intent.
matchApplication: Forwards, midfielders and defenders frequently make multiple leads before receiving possession. This drill develops the capacity to recover, reposition and present again rather than stopping after an unsuccessful or completed effort.

title: Multi-Directional Football Conditioning
objective: Develop controlled movement in multiple directions while maintaining football awareness and clean possession skills.
groundSize: Four to six grids measuring 15 metres by 15 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place one cone in the centre of each grid.
Place four different coloured cones around the outside.
Position one feeder outside the grid.
Organise two to four working players per grid.
Give the feeder one football.
Set work periods of 25 seconds and recovery periods of 40 seconds.
howTheDrillWorks:
The working player begins at the centre cone.
The feeder calls a colour and delivers a handball.
The player receives, moves to the nominated cone and returns the handball.
The player returns towards the centre.
The feeder calls a different colour.
The player must use the appropriate movement pattern: forward run, lateral shuffle, diagonal movement or controlled backward movement.
Continue for 25 seconds.
Rotate the feeder and worker.
Complete four to six repetitions.
In the final round, the feeder may use visual signals instead of verbal calls.
coachingPoints: Keep the body balanced through every change of direction.
Use short steps when decelerating.
Avoid crossing the feet during lateral movement.
Turn the hips before accelerating diagonally.
Keep eyes on the feeder.
Present hands early.
Return the football accurately.
Maintain movement quality rather than chasing excessive speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players react accurately to the cue.
Whether movement mechanics change between directions.
Whether players lose sight of the football.
Whether handball accuracy remains consistent.
Whether fatigue causes uncontrolled footwork.

commonErrors.error: Player crosses feet during lateral movement.
commonErrors.correction: Use short shuffle steps and maintain a stable base.

commonErrors.error: Player turns away from the feeder.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest partially open to the football.

commonErrors.error: Movement becomes rushed and unbalanced.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed and widen the change-of-direction area.

commonErrors.error: Player guesses the next cone.
commonErrors.correction: Require a pause at the centre until the cue is given.

commonErrors.error: Handballs become inaccurate late in the interval.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the work period or increase recovery.

progressions: Add a second football.
Use only visual cues.
Add a disposal choice at the outside cone.
Increase work time to 30 seconds.
Introduce a passive defender in the grid.
regressions: Complete the drill without a football.
successIndicators: Maintain visual connection with the football.
matchApplication: Australian football movement is rarely straight-line only. Players shuffle, backtrack, turn, accelerate and change angles while tracking the football. This drill develops conditioning through those varied movement demands.

title: Fundamental Load Management Circuit
objective: Teach players and coaches to adjust football-conditioning volume, intensity and recovery while maintaining safe movement and skill quality.
groundSize: Approximately one-third of an oval.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create three workload stations:
Green Station: Low-intensity continuous handball and support movement.
Amber Station: Moderate kick-mark-run pattern.
Red Station: Short acceleration and disposal efforts.
Divide players into three groups. Set three-minute station periods with one minute of walking recovery and feedback between stations.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete three minutes at the Green Station.
At the end, players provide a simple effort rating from one to five.
Players walk for one minute and rotate to the Amber Station.
Players complete three minutes of moderate running and kicking.
Players again provide an effort rating and identify whether skill quality changed.
Players rotate to the Red Station.
Players complete short high-intensity efforts with full technical control.
Coaches compare visible movement quality, disposal accuracy and player effort ratings.
After all stations, groups repeat one station at an adjusted workload.
Coaches may shorten distance, reduce repetitions or increase recovery based on the feedback.
coachingPoints: Explain the difference between volume, intensity and recovery.
Encourage honest player feedback.
Do not reward players for reporting the highest effort.
Compare physical effort with skill quality.
Adjust workload for age, position and training history.
Recognise early signs of technical deterioration.
Keep all recovery active.
Use the circuit to teach workload awareness rather than simply create fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether player ratings match visible effort.
Whether technique deteriorates at a particular station.
Whether players understand different workload types.
Whether recovery needs vary between groups.
Whether modified players can complete an appropriate version.

commonErrors.error: Players rate every station as maximal.
commonErrors.correction: Explain the rating scale and provide clear examples.

commonErrors.error: Coaches ignore player feedback.
commonErrors.correction: Compare feedback with movement and skill observations before adjusting.

commonErrors.error: Red Station volume is excessive.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce repetitions and protect high-quality movement.

commonErrors.error: Modified players complete the same load as fully conditioned players.
commonErrors.correction: Create individual distance, duration or recovery targets.

commonErrors.error: Players stand still during recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Require walking, breathing control and preparation for the next station.

progressions: Use heart-rate or GPS data where available.
Allow player leaders to recommend workload adjustments.
Add a second circuit with revised work-to-rest ratios.
Use positional workload stations.
Record individual results across several weeks.
successIndicators: Understand the purpose of each workload.
Maintain safe movement and skill quality.
matchApplication: Players and coaches must manage conditioning loads across training, matches and recovery periods. Understanding when quality is declining helps prevent ineffective fatigue and supports consistent football performance.

title: Conditioning Fundamentals Consolidation Game
primarySkill: Applying conditioning fundamentals in a continuous football game
objective: Consolidate the fundamental conditioning behaviours developed in CF-001 to CF-019 within a continuous, competitive and football-relevant activity.
groundSize: A 60-metre by 45-metre area divided into three horizontal zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide players into two even teams.
Mark defensive, central and attacking zones.
Place two scoring gates at each end.
Begin with one football.
Nominate one player from each team as a rotating recovery player.
Use three-minute playing periods with one-minute active recovery.
Apply controlled contact or touch pressure depending on the group.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams attempt to move the football through all three zones and score by kicking or handballing through an end gate.
Players may not remain in the same zone after disposing; they must support into another zone.
A turnover requires the team that lost possession to recover into defensive positions.
A score is worth one point.
A bonus point is awarded when the scoring team completes the possession with no stationary players.
The rotating recovery player walks along the boundary for 30 seconds before re-entering.
Players rotate through the recovery role.
Play for three minutes.
During the one-minute recovery, teams walk, control breathing and discuss spacing.
Complete four to six playing periods.
Coaches assess movement quality, skill execution, recovery behaviour and effort consistency.
coachingPoints: Use sustainable movement between high-intensity efforts.
Accelerate when creating or closing space.
Decelerate under control before receiving or disposing.
Move immediately after releasing the football.
Maintain width and depth.
Recover quickly after turnovers.
Use active recovery between periods.
Preserve skill quality as fatigue builds.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players vary their running tempo effectively.
Whether support movement continues after disposal.
Whether players recover defensively after turnovers.
Whether skill quality remains acceptable.
Whether players use active recovery periods well.
Whether movement becomes congested as fatigue increases.
Whether players communicate during both work and recovery.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint continuously without purpose.
commonErrors.correction: Coach controlled running between decisive efforts.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after disposing.
commonErrors.correction: Apply the rule requiring movement into another zone.

commonErrors.error: Turnovers create no defensive reaction.
commonErrors.correction: Award the opposition a bonus point when recovery is delayed.

commonErrors.error: Players crowd the central zone.
commonErrors.correction: Require minimum numbers in the outside zones.

commonErrors.error: Recovery periods become inactive.
commonErrors.correction: Require walking, breathing control and brief tactical communication.

commonErrors.error: Skill quality collapses late in the game.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery or shorten playing periods.

progressions: Add a second football.
Reduce active recovery periods.
Increase controlled defensive pressure.
Require a minimum number of disposals in each zone.
Add positional roles and match-specific starting structures.
regressions: Shorten playing periods to two minutes.
Allow additional recovery for modified players.
successIndicators: Move continuously without unnecessary maximal running.
matchApplication: This game combines the conditioning fundamentals required in Australian football: continuous movement, controlled pacing, decisive acceleration, safe braking, repeat involvement, disposal under fatigue and active recovery between efforts.

title: Change-of-Pace Possession Run
primarySkill: Changing running pace while maintaining possession involvement
objective: Develop the ability to move efficiently at different running speeds and accelerate at the correct moment to support or receive possession.
groundSize: Four to six lanes measuring 45 metres by 10 metres.
equipment: Three different coloured marker cones per lane
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark three movement sections in each lane.
Use one colour for controlled jogging, one for steady running and one for acceleration.
Position two players at each end of every lane.
Place one supporting player midway along the lane.
Allocate one football to each lane.
Establish a continuous rotation in which players follow their disposal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player carries the football through the controlled-jog section.
On reaching the second colour, the player increases to a steady running pace.
At the acceleration marker, the player handballs to the central support player and accelerates past.
The central player returns the football into the runner’s path.
The runner completes a short kick to the player leading from the opposite end.
All players follow their disposal and rotate forward.
Continue for two minutes.
Walk for 40 seconds.
Repeat in the opposite direction.
Complete four work periods, changing the acceleration location between rounds.
coachingPoints: Match running speed to the designated section.
Avoid sprinting during the controlled movement phase.
Accelerate decisively when passing the final marker.
Deliver the handball in front of the moving support player.
Continue past possession after handballing.
Regain balance before kicking.
Communicate the pace change and receiving option.
Maintain similar skill quality at every speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players genuinely alter their running speed.
Whether acceleration occurs at the correct marker.
Whether support timing matches the pace change.
Whether players remain balanced before kicking.
Whether disposal accuracy changes when speed increases.

commonErrors.error: Players run at one speed throughout.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce the purpose of each coloured movement section.

commonErrors.error: Acceleration begins too early.
commonErrors.correction: Require players to hold tempo until both feet pass the final marker.

commonErrors.error: Support player waits flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Begin moving as the ball carrier enters the steady-running section.

commonErrors.error: Return handball is delivered behind the runner.
commonErrors.correction: Release earlier and target the runner’s forward side.

commonErrors.error: Final kick is rushed.
commonErrors.correction: Require two balanced steps before disposal.

progressions: Change the pace sequence on the coach’s call.
Add a passive trailing defender.
Include a ground-ball receive before the final kick.
Reduce recovery between work periods.
Add a second support player and disposal choice.
successIndicators: Change speed at the designated points.
Complete repeated work periods without losing movement control.
matchApplication: Players rarely run at one constant speed during Australian football. Effective players conserve energy during lower-intensity movement and accelerate when space, possession or defensive pressure requires a decisive effort.

title: Overlap Running Chain
objective: Develop the ability to dispose of the football, accelerate past the receiver and remain involved through repeated overlap movements.
groundSize: Three to six channels measuring 40 metres by 10 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark starting, middle and end stations in each channel.
Place one player at the middle station and one at the end station.
Position the remaining players at the start.
Give the first player at the start a football.
Mark a two-metre-wide overlap lane beside the direct possession line.
Allow sufficient space beyond the end station for controlled deceleration.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A carries the football towards Player B at the middle station.
Player A handballs to Player B and immediately accelerates through the overlap lane.
Player B takes two or three steps and returns the football to Player A.
Player A continues forward and handballs to Player C at the end station.
Player B then overlaps Player C and receives the return handball.
The chain continues back in the opposite direction.
Players follow their disposal and rotate into the next station.
Continue for 35 seconds.
Walk for 45 seconds.
Complete five or six repetitions.
coachingPoints: Accelerate immediately after releasing the football.
Use a clear overlap lane outside the receiver.
Handball to the runner’s forward side.
Do not drift behind the ball carrier.
Maintain enough width to avoid collisions.
Keep the football moving ahead of the running chain.
Communicate before every receive.
Control speed before the end station.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players accelerate after disposal.
Whether the overlap runner creates genuine separation.
Whether the return handball is timed correctly.
Whether the chain remains moving forward.
Whether fatigue causes players to shorten or abandon the overlap.

commonErrors.error: Player handballs and remains behind the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Make the overlap lane compulsory after every disposal.

commonErrors.error: Overlap runner passes too close to the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one to two metres of lateral width.

commonErrors.error: Return handball is released too late.
commonErrors.correction: Deliver as the runner reaches the receiver’s shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Players run into the end station at full speed.
commonErrors.correction: Add a deceleration zone beyond the final cone.

commonErrors.error: Chain becomes stationary after an error.
commonErrors.correction: Reset quickly from the nearest station and continue the work period.

progressions: Add a passive defender tracking the overlap.
Require the final possession to be kicked through a target gate.
Increase work periods to 45 seconds.
Add a second football in larger groups.
Allow the receiver to choose whether to return the handball or continue carrying.
successIndicators: Repeat the pattern without major technical decline.
matchApplication: Overlap running allows teams to create an extra player around possession, break lines and move the football beyond pressure. This drill conditions players to keep running after their first involvement.

title: Width-to-Corridor Conditioning
primarySkill: Repeated lateral and forward movement between width and corridor
objective: Develop the running capacity and positioning habits required to move the football from outside width into the corridor and continue supporting forward movement.
groundSize: A 60-metre by 50-metre area divided into two wide channels and one central corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a 15-metre-wide corridor through the centre.
Mark two outside channels along each boundary side of the area.
Position players in groups of five or six.
Begin each group with possession in one outside channel.
Place a target player at the opposite end.
